questions.knowledge_point: Reducing a First-Order ODE to a Separable Form by Factoring and Using a Linear Substitution
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3x+6y.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =3(x+2y).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1) & =3z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=6z+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=6z+1.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x+8y-1}{4}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+4y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(x+4y)-1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+4y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+4\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1).
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1) & =\frac{2z-1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2z.$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2{sin}^{2}⁡(3x+3y)-1.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(g(x,y))=-6x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(3(x+y))-1\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =2{sin}^{2}⁡(3z)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2{sin}^{2}⁡(3z).
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{csc}^{2}⁡(3z)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =2 \\ \int {csc}^{2}⁡(3z)\,\text{d}z & =\int 2\,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{cot}⁡(3z) & =2x+K \\ \operatorname{cot}⁡(3z) & =-6x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-3K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cot}⁡(3x+3y)=-6x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=3x+3y.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2x-2y).
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=6x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2(x-y))\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2z)\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3\operatorname{sec}⁡(2z).
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2z)\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3 \\ \int \operatorname{cos}⁡(2z)\,\text{d}z & =\int 3\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2z) & =3x+K \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2z) & =6x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-2y)=6x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x-2y).
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{10x+2y}{5x+y+1}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=5x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2(5x+y)}{(5x+y)+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=5x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=5+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-5.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-5 & =\frac{2z}{z+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{7z+5}{z+1}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{7z+5}{z+1}.$
